7. Denoising

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Denoising estimates a clean signal from measurements corrupted by noise. Its central difficulty is to suppress random fluctuations without erasing edges, textures, or other features of the underlying signal. We model common acquisition noise, compare linear filters with nonlinear thresholding, analyze how regularity and sparsity govern reconstruction error, and adapt the methods to Poisson and multiplicative noise.

7.1 Noise Modeling¶

7.1.1 Noise in Images¶

Figure 7.1 illustrates the variety of imaging noise. Different acquisition devices produce different noise statistics, while the images themselves vary in smoothness and geometry.

Figure 7.1. Gaussian, Poisson, and multiplicative Gamma noise simulated on the same flower image.

The model should reflect both the acquisition process and the noise statistics. The regularity and geometry of the clean signal then guide the choice of a basis for its representation.

Since noise perturbs discrete measurements from acquisition devices, we consider only finite-dimensional real signals f∈RNf\in\mathbb{R}^Nf∈RN.

7.1.2 Image Formation¶

Figure 7.2 summarizes the model: a clean image f0f_0f0​ combines with noise www to produce the observation Y:=f0⊕wY := f_0 \oplus wY:=f0​⊕w. The operation ⊕\oplus⊕ may be addition or multiplication. The observed image YYY is modeled as a random vector.

Figure 7.2. Image acquisition, noise, and reconstruction by denoising.

In the statistical model, www is a random vector with a specified distribution. A numerical experiment uses one realization, also written www.

Additive Noise.

The simplest image formation model adds noise to a clean signal f0f_0f0​

Y:=f0+wY := f_0 + wY:=f0​+w

where www is the noise residual. Both www and YYY are random; an acquired image is one realization of YYY, denoted by yyy or fff below. Figures 7.3 and 7.4 illustrate additive noise on a signal and an image.

Figure 7.3. One-dimensional additive Gaussian noise at low, medium, and high levels, with a common clean signal and normalized noise realization.

Figure 7.4. Two-dimensional additive noise: the clean image f0f_0f0​ and the observation f=f0+wf=f_0+wf=f0​+w, with w∼N(0,σ2I)w\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2 I)w∼N(0,σ2I).

The simplest model assumes independent centered Gaussian entries wnw_nwn​ with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2: w∼N(0,σ2IdN)w\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2\mathrm{Id}_N)w∼N(0,σ2IdN​). This is Gaussian white noise.

Depending on the image acquisition device, other noise distributions may be appropriate, including uniform noise wn∈[−a,a]w_n \in [-a,a]wn​∈[−a,a] or heavy-tailed generalized Gaussian noise with density

pw(u)∝e−∣u/s∣α,s>0,0<α<2.p_w(u)\propto e^{-|u/s|^\alpha},\qquad s>0,\quad0<\alpha<2.pw​(u)∝e−∣u/s∣α,s>0,0<α<2.

In many situations, the noise is not additive; its intensity may, for instance, depend on the signal intensity. This is the case with the Poisson and multiplicative noise models considered in Section 7.4.

7.1.3 Denoiser¶

A denoiser produces an estimate f~=D(Y)\tilde f = \mathcal{D}(Y)f~​=D(Y) of f0f_0f0​ from the observation YYY alone. The map D\mathcal{D}D is deterministic, but its output is random because it depends on the noise www. With centered additive noise, YYY has mean f0f_0f0​, so denoising estimates that mean from a single realization. Figure 7.5 illustrates the result.

The quality of a denoiser is measured using the mean squared risk Ew∣ ⁣∣f0−f~∣ ⁣∣2\mathbb E_w|\!| f_0-\tilde f |\!|^2Ew​∣∣f0​−f~​∣∣2, where Ew\mathbb E_wEw​ averages over the noise www. This risk is a theoretical quantity because f0f_0f0​ is unknown in practice. In experiments with known clean data, we instead evaluate one realization y∼Y=f0+wy \sim Y = f_0 + wy∼Y=f0​+w using the signal-to-noise ratio SNR(D(y),f0)\text{SNR}(\mathcal{D}(y),f_0)SNR(D(y),f0​), defined by

SNR(f,g):=−20log⁡10(∣ ⁣∣f−g∣ ⁣∣/∣ ⁣∣g∣ ⁣∣).\text{SNR}(f,g) := -20\log_{10}( |\!| f-g |\!|/|\!| g |\!| ).SNR(f,g):=−20log10​(∣∣f−g∣∣/∣∣g∣∣).

The SNR is measured in decibels (dB). Computing it requires the clean signal f0f_0f0​, so it serves as a benchmark in controlled experiments. Because an ℓ2\ell^2ℓ2 error does not fully describe perceptual quality, visual inspection should accompany the numerical comparison.

Figure 7.5. Left: clean image, center: noisy image, right: denoised image.

7.2 Linear Denoising by Filtering¶

7.2.1 Translation Invariant Estimators¶

A linear estimator D(Y)=f~\mathcal{D}(Y) = \tilde fD(Y)=f~​ of f0f_0f0​ preserves addition, D(f+g)=D(f)+D(g)\mathcal{D}(f+g) = \mathcal{D}(f)+\mathcal{D}(g)D(f+g)=D(f)+D(g), and scalar multiplication. A translation-invariant estimator commutes with translations: D(fτ)=D(f)τ\mathcal{D}(f_\tau) = \mathcal{D}(f)_\tauD(fτ​)=D(f)τ​, where fτ(t)=f(t−τ)f_\tau(t) = f(t-\tau)fτ​(t)=f(t−τ). We assume periodic boundary conditions, in either one or two dimensions.

An estimator with both properties is a convolution filter:

D(f)=f⋆h\mathcal{D}(f) = f \star hD(f)=f⋆h

where h∈RNh\in\mathbb{R}^Nh∈RN is a filter. Denoising filters are usually low-pass. To preserve constant signals, one imposes

∑nhn=h^0=1\sum_n h_n = \hat h_0 = 1n∑​hn​=h^0​=1

where h^\hat hh^ is the discrete Fourier transform.

Figure 7.6 illustrates denoising with a low-pass filter.

Figure 7.6. Gaussian filtering: noisy signal, kernel, and filtered signal (top), with their Fourier magnitudes below.

The filtering strength is usually controlled by the width sss of hhh. A typical example is the (discretized) Gaussian filter

∀ −N/2<i⩽N/2,hs,i=1Zsexp⁡(−i22s2)(7.1)\forall \,-N/2 < i \leqslant N/2, \quad h_{s,i} = \frac{1}{Z_s} \exp\left( -\frac{ i^2 }{ 2s^2} \right) \tag{7.1}∀−N/2<i⩽N/2,hs,i​=Zs​1​exp(−2s2i2​)(7.1)

where ZsZ_sZs​ normalizes the filter so that ∑ihs,i=1\sum_i h_{s,i}=1∑i​hs,i​=1, preserving constant signals. Figure 7.6 shows the effect of Gaussian filtering in the spatial and Fourier domains.

Figure 7.7 shows the effect of increasing the filter width sss. Linear filtering works well on smooth signals, but removing more noise also blurs edges and other singularities.

Figure 7.7. Gaussian filtering with increasing width: three signals (top) and five images (bottom).

7.2.2 Optimal Filter Selection and Bias-Variance Tradeoff¶

The best filter depends on both the unknown signal f0f_0f0​ and the noise level σ\sigmaσ. Rather than optimize over all filters, we can tune a width parameter sss within a family such as the Gaussian filters in (7.1).

The triangle inequality separates the smoothing error from the remaining noise:

∣ ⁣∣f~−f0∣ ⁣∣⩽∣ ⁣∣hs⋆f0−f0∣ ⁣∣+∣ ⁣∣hs⋆w∣ ⁣∣|\!| \tilde f - f_0 |\!| \leqslant|\!| h_s \star f_0 - f_0 |\!| + |\!| h_s \star w |\!|∣∣f~​−f0​∣∣⩽∣∣hs​⋆f0​−f0​∣∣+∣∣hs​⋆w∣∣

The filter width sss balances noise removal against excessive smoothing of singularities. A wider filter typically reduces ∣ ⁣∣hs⋆w∣ ⁣∣|\!| h_s \star w |\!|∣∣hs​⋆w∣∣ while increasing ∣ ⁣∣hs⋆f0−f0∣ ⁣∣|\!| h_s\star f_0-f_0 |\!|∣∣hs​⋆f0​−f0​∣∣.

Figure 7.8 shows the SNR as a function of filter width, evaluated using the known clean signal.

Figure 7.8. SNR as a function of filter width for a signal (left) and an image (right).

Figure 7.9 uses the width s⋆s^\stars⋆ that maximizes SNR for the displayed observation. This choice uses the known clean signal to assess the best achievable result within the filter family.

Figure 7.9. Gaussian filtering at the SNR-optimal widths. From left to right: noisy signal, filtered signal, noisy image, and filtered image.

Some noise remains at the SNR-optimal width. Increasing the filter width introduces strong blur and reduces the SNR, although the result may look more pleasant.

7.2.3 Oracle Denoiser¶

To study the best possible choice of hhh, first suppose that an oracle knows the clean signal f0f_0f0​.

Recall the model Y=f0+wY = f_0 + wY=f0​+w, where www is Gaussian white noise: wk∼N(0,σ2)w_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)wk​∼N(0,σ2) and the wkw_kwk​ are independent and identically distributed. The clean signal f0f_0f0​ is fixed. Choose an orthonormal basis (ψk)k(\psi_k)_k(ψk​)k​, typically the Fourier basis, and restrict attention to linear estimators that are diagonal in it:

f~≔∑kλk⟨Y, ψk⟩ ψk.(7.2)\tilde{f} \coloneqq \sum_k \lambda_k \langle Y,\,\psi_k\rangle \, \psi_k. \tag{7.2}f~​:=k∑​λk​⟨Y,ψk​⟩ψk​.(7.2)

For the Fourier basis, this means f~=Y⋆h\tilde{f} = Y \star hf~​=Y⋆h where h^=λ\hat h=\lambdah^=λ. Note that f~\tilde{f}f~​ is a random vector.

The oracle may use f0f_0f0​ to select the gains λ\lambdaλ, but the estimator must still be linear in YYY and have the displayed diagonal form. It cannot simply return f0f_0f0​.

Denoting ck≔⟨f0, ψk⟩c_k \coloneqq \langle f_0,\,\psi_k\rangleck​:=⟨f0​,ψk​⟩ (for the normalized discrete Fourier basis, c=f^0/Nc=\hat f_0/\sqrt Nc=f^​0​/N​), the expected risk of this denoiser is

Ew∥f~−f0∥2=∑kEw∣⟨f~−f0, ψk⟩∣2=∑kEw∣λk(ck+⟨w, ψk⟩)−ck∣2.\mathbb{E}_w \|\tilde{f} - f_0\|^2 = \sum_k \mathbb{E}_w \left| \langle \tilde{f} - f_0,\,\psi_k\rangle \right|^2 = \sum_k \mathbb{E}_w \left| \lambda_k \left( c_k + \langle w,\,\psi_k\rangle \right) - c_k \right|^2 .Ew​∥f~​−f0​∥2=k∑​Ew​∣∣​⟨f~​−f0​,ψk​⟩∣∣​2=k∑​Ew​∣λk​(ck​+⟨w,ψk​⟩)−ck​∣2.

For a real orthonormal basis, the transformed noise is again independent Gaussian noise with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. For a complex unitary Fourier basis applied to real noise, each coefficient still has second moment σ2\sigma^2σ2, which suffices here, although conjugate-frequency coefficients are dependent. By expanding the square and using E(⟨w, ψk⟩)=0\mathbb{E}(\langle w,\,\psi_k\rangle) = 0E(⟨w,ψk​⟩)=0, we obtain

Ew∥f~−f0∥2=∑k(∣ck∣2∣λk−1∣2+∣λk∣2σ2).\mathbb{E}_w \|\tilde{f} - f_0\|^2 = \sum_k\left(|c_k|^2|\lambda_k-1|^2+|\lambda_k|^2\sigma^2\right) .Ew​∥f~​−f0​∥2=k∑​(∣ck​∣2∣λk​−1∣2+∣λk​∣2σ2).

Knowing ckc_kck​, the oracle minimizes Ew(∥f~−f0∥2)\mathbb{E}_w \left( \|\tilde{f} - f_0\|^2 \right)Ew​(∥f~​−f0​∥2) over λ\lambdaλ. The minimization separates over the indices kkk:

min⁡λk(∣ck∣2∣λk−1∣2+∣λk∣2σ2).\min_{\lambda_k} \left( |c_k|^2 |\lambda_k - 1|^2 + |\lambda_k|^2 \sigma^2 \right).λk​min​(∣ck​∣2∣λk​−1∣2+∣λk​∣2σ2).

The solution thus satisfies

∣ck∣2(λk−1)+λkσ2=0,|c_k|^2 (\lambda_k - 1) + \lambda_k \sigma^2 = 0,∣ck​∣2(λk​−1)+λk​σ2=0,

i.e.,

λk=∣ck∣2∣ck∣2+σ2.\lambda_k = \frac{|c_k|^2}{|c_k|^2+\sigma^2}.λk​=∣ck​∣2+σ2∣ck​∣2​.

If σ=0\sigma = 0σ=0, choosing λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 gives the identity map. When ∣ck∣|c_k|∣ck​∣ decays, increasing σ\sigmaσ suppresses the weaker coefficients more strongly, concentrating the gains on the dominant signal components.

7.2.4 Wiener Filter¶

We now replace access to the clean signal by a known probability model for it.

Suppose both the noise w∼Ww \sim Ww∼W and the clean signal f0∼Ff_0 \sim Ff0​∼F have known distributions. We seek a filter minimizing the error averaged over both sources of randomness, assuming WWW and FFF are independent.

We assume D\mathcal{D}D has the form (7.2).

The optimal hhh thus minimizes

Ew,F∥D(F+w)−F∥2\mathbb{E}_{w,F} \|\mathcal{D}(F+w) - F\|^2Ew,F​∥D(F+w)−F∥2

Independence of WWW and FFF allows the same risk calculation:

Ew,F∥D(F+w)−F∥2=∑k(αk∣λk−1∣2+∣λk∣2σ2)whereαk:=EF∣⟨F, ψk⟩∣2\mathbb{E}_{w,F} \|\mathcal{D}(F+w)-F\|^2=\sum_k\left(\alpha_k|\lambda_k-1|^2+|\lambda_k|^2\sigma^2\right) \quad\text{where}\quad \alpha_k := \mathbb{E}_{F} |\langle F,\,\psi_k\rangle|^2Ew,F​∥D(F+w)−F∥2=k∑​(αk​∣λk​−1∣2+∣λk​∣2σ2)whereαk​:=EF​∣⟨F,ψk​⟩∣2

The optimal filter thus has coefficients

λk=αkαk+σ2.(7.3)\lambda_k=\frac{\alpha_k}{\alpha_k+\sigma^2}. \tag{7.3}λk​=αk​+σ2αk​​.(7.3)

Relative to the oracle filter, the individual energy ∣ck∣2|c_k|^2∣ck​∣2 is replaced by the expected coefficient energy αk⩾0\alpha_k\geqslant 0αk​⩾0, the signal power spectrum in the Fourier basis.

This filter is known as the Wiener filter.

For the normalized discrete Fourier basis, αk=N−1E∣F^k∣2\alpha_k=N^{-1}\mathbb E|\hat F_k|^2αk​=N−1E∣F^k​∣2. Define the averaged autocorrelation

ηj=1NE∑n=0N−1FnFn−j‾,αk=η^k.\eta_j=\frac1N\mathbb E\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}F_n\overline{F_{n-j}}, \qquad\alpha_k=\hat\eta_k.ηj​=N1​En=0∑N−1​Fn​Fn−j​​,αk​=η^​k​.

Here indices are periodic and η^\hat\etaη^​ uses the unnormalized DFT of Chapter 2. This normalization is needed because the Fourier atoms used in the risk calculation have unit norm.

So far, D\mathcal{D}D has been restricted to the basis ψm\psi_mψm​ through the diagonal form (7.2). If FFF is stationary, its law is unchanged by shifts: F(⋅−τ)F(\cdot-\tau)F(⋅−τ) has the same law as FFF. In that case, the Fourier Wiener filter (7.3) is optimal among all linear denoisers, even without imposing a diagonal form in advance.

An empirical estimate based on one noisy realization is N−1∣y^k∣2N^{-1}|\hat y_k|^2N−1∣y^​k​∣2. Its expectation is αk+σ2\alpha_k+\sigma^2αk​+σ2, and its variance can be large. Empirical Wiener methods therefore need noise subtraction, nonnegativity constraints, and usually additional smoothing or a signal model.

7.2.5 Denoising and Linear Approximation¶

Approximation theory, developed in Chapter 5, provides a different route to denoising bounds. It requires a class of clean signals rather than a probability distribution on that class.

Fix an orthonormal basis B=(ψm)m\mathcal{B}= (\psi_m)_mB=(ψm​)m​ of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN. A simple estimator retains only the first MMM coefficients of the noisy observation in B\mathcal{B}B:

D(f)=f~:=∑m=1M⟨f, ψm⟩ψm.(7.4)\mathcal{D}(f) = \tilde f \mathrel{:=}\sum_{m=1}^M \langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle \psi_m. \tag{7.4}D(f)=f~​:=m=1∑M​⟨f,ψm​⟩ψm​.(7.4)

This is a linear projection onto the space spanned by (ψm)m=1M(\psi_m)_{m=1}^M(ψm​)m=1M​.

This denoising scheme is parameterized by the number 1⩽M⩽N1\leqslant M\leqslant N1⩽M⩽N of retained coefficients. Increasing MMM retains more signal detail but also more noise.

For the discrete Fourier basis ordered by increasing frequency, this is ideal low-pass filtering by convolution with a discrete Dirichlet kernel.

This is the special case of (7.2) in which the gains λm\lambda_mλm​ are binary, λm∈{0,1}\lambda_m \in \{0,1\}λm​∈{0,1}. Although restrictive, this choice yields useful rates under the approximation assumptions of Theorem 7.1. It requires a regularity model for f0f_0f0​, but does not assume a random signal distribution FFF.

The proof is finite-dimensional, but its bound has no explicit dependence on NNN. Extending it to a continuum model requires interpreting white noise as a generalized random process.

Theorem 7.1

Assume σ>0\sigma>0σ>0, β>0\beta>0β>0, and

∣ ⁣∣f0−f0,Mlin∣ ⁣∣2⩽CM−2β,f0,Mlin=∑m=1M⟨f0, ψm⟩ψm,1⩽M⩽N.|\!| f_0-f_{0,M}^{\mathrm{lin}} |\!|^2\leqslant CM^{-2\beta},\qquad f_{0,M}^{\mathrm{lin}}=\sum_{m=1}^M\langle f_0,\,\psi_m\rangle\psi_m, \quad1\leqslant M\leqslant N.∣∣f0​−f0,Mlin​∣∣2⩽CM−2β,f0,Mlin​=m=1∑M​⟨f0​,ψm​⟩ψm​,1⩽M⩽N.

The projection denoiser (7.4) has risk

E∣ ⁣∣f0−f~∣ ⁣∣2=Mσ2+∣ ⁣∣f0−f0,Mlin∣ ⁣∣2.\mathbb E|\!| f_0-\tilde f |\!|^2=M\sigma^2+|\!| f_0-f_{0,M}^{\mathrm{lin}} |\!|^2.E∣∣f0​−f~​∣∣2=Mσ2+∣∣f0​−f0,Mlin​∣∣2.

If 0<σ2⩽C0<\sigma^2\leqslant C0<σ2⩽C, choose

t=(C/σ2)1/(2β+1),M=min⁡{N,⌈t⌉}.(7.5)t=(C/\sigma^2)^{1/(2\beta+1)},\qquad M=\min\{N,\lceil t\rceil\}. \tag{7.5}t=(C/σ2)1/(2β+1),M=min{N,⌈t⌉}.(7.5)

Then

E∣ ⁣∣f0−f~∣ ⁣∣2⩽3C1/(2β+1)σ4β/(2β+1).\mathbb E|\!| f_0-\tilde f |\!|^2\leqslant 3C^{1/(2\beta+1)}\sigma^{4\beta/(2\beta+1)}.E∣∣f0​−f~​∣∣2⩽3C1/(2β+1)σ4β/(2β+1).
Proof

Orthogonality separates retained noise coefficients from discarded signal coefficients. Each retained noise coefficient has variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, which proves the risk identity. If t⩽Nt\leqslant Nt⩽N, then t⩽M⩽2tt\leqslant M\leqslant 2tt⩽M⩽2t and

Mσ2+CM−2β⩽2tσ2+Ct−2β=3C1/(2β+1)σ4β/(2β+1).M\sigma^2+CM^{-2\beta}\leqslant 2t\sigma^2+Ct^{-2\beta}=3C^{1/(2\beta+1)}\sigma^{4\beta/(2\beta+1)}.Mσ2+CM−2β⩽2tσ2+Ct−2β=3C1/(2β+1)σ4β/(2β+1).

If t>Nt>Nt>N, the estimator retains all coefficients and its risk is Nσ2⩽tσ2N\sigma^2\leqslant t\sigma^2Nσ2⩽tσ2, which obeys the same bound.

Several observations help interpret this result:

  • The approximation assumption bounds the denoising error E(∣ ⁣∣f0−f~∣ ⁣∣2)\mathbb E(|\!| f_0 - \tilde f |\!|^2)E(∣∣f0​−f~​∣∣2) independently of the sample count NNN, even though the total input noise energy E(∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣2)=Nσ2\mathbb E(|\!| w |\!|^2)=N\sigma^2E(∣∣w∣∣2)=Nσ2 grows with NNN.

  • A larger approximation exponent β\betaβ gives faster decay of the error as σ\sigmaσ tends to zero. The exponent approaches that of the parametric rate σ2\sigma^2σ2 as β\betaβ increases.

  • The proof uses a finite sample count NNN. White noise with constant positive variance in every coordinate has infinite energy in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, although other random vectors may have finite energy. The balancing choice applies when N⩾tN\geqslant tN⩾t; otherwise the estimator is the identity. A continuum interpretation as σ→0\sigma\to0σ→0 also requires increasing the sampling resolution.

  • Section 5.3.1 bounds approximation errors for continuous signal and image models. To transfer these bounds to sampled data, choose NNN large enough that discretization error is smaller than denoising error.

The Sobolev model in Section 5.2.1 provides a useful example. For discrete signals with an increasing sample count NNN, especially as σ\sigmaσ decreases, a compatible weighted coefficient bound gives the same approximation argument as Proposition 5.3.

Let α>0\alpha>0α>0. If

∑m=1Nm2α∣⟨f0, ψm⟩∣2⩽C(7.6)\sum_{m=1}^N m^{2\alpha} |\langle f_0,\,\psi_m\rangle|^{2} \leqslant C \tag{7.6}m=1∑N​m2α∣⟨f0​,ψm​⟩∣2⩽C(7.6)

then

∀ M∈{1,…,N},∣ ⁣∣f0−f0,Mlin∣ ⁣∣2⩽CM−2α\forall \,M\in\{1,\ldots,N\}, \quad |\!| f_0 - f_{0,M}^{\text{lin}} |\!|^2 \leqslant C M^{-2\alpha}∀M∈{1,…,N},∣∣f0​−f0,Mlin​∣∣2⩽CM−2α
Proof
C⩾∑m=1Nm2α∣⟨f0, ψm⟩∣2⩾∑m>Mm2α∣⟨f0, ψm⟩∣2⩾M2α∑m>M∣⟨f0, ψm⟩∣2⩾M2α∣ ⁣∣f0−f0,Mlin∣ ⁣∣2.C \geqslant\sum_{m=1}^N m^{2\alpha} |\langle f_0,\,\psi_m\rangle|^{2} \geqslant\sum_{m>M} m^{2\alpha} |\langle f_0,\,\psi_m\rangle|^{2} \geqslant M^{2\alpha} \sum_{m>M} |\langle f_0,\,\psi_m\rangle|^{2} \geqslant M^{2\alpha} |\!| f_0 - f_{0,M}^{\text{lin}} |\!|^2.C⩾m=1∑N​m2α∣⟨f0​,ψm​⟩∣2⩾m>M∑​m2α∣⟨f0​,ψm​⟩∣2⩾M2αm>M∑​∣⟨f0​,ψm​⟩∣2⩾M2α∣∣f0​−f0,Mlin​∣∣2.

For normalized Fourier atoms ordered by increasing physical frequency, an appropriately scaled discrete weighted-energy bound approximates the periodic Sobolev model. The sample normalization, frequency weights, and boundary convention must match those of the continuous signal. Under this compatibility, low-frequency projection efficiently denoises smooth signals and images.

7.3 Nonlinear Denoising by Thresholding¶

7.3.1 Hard Thresholding¶

We consider a real orthonormal basis {ψm}m\{\psi_m\}_m{ψm​}m​ of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN, for instance a discrete wavelet basis.

The noisy coefficients satisfy

⟨f, ψm⟩=⟨f0, ψm⟩+⟨w, ψm⟩.(7.7)\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle = \langle f_0,\,\psi_m\rangle + \langle w,\,\psi_m\rangle. \tag{7.7}⟨f,ψm​⟩=⟨f0​,ψm​⟩+⟨w,ψm​⟩.(7.7)

Orthogonal transforms preserve Gaussian white noise, so the coefficients ⟨w, ψm⟩\langle w,\,\psi_m\rangle⟨w,ψm​⟩ remain independent centered Gaussians with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. If the basis {ψm}m\{\psi_m\}_m{ψm​}m​ represents f0f_0f0​ sparsely, most clean coefficients ⟨f0, ψm⟩\langle f_0,\,\psi_m\rangle⟨f0​,ψm​⟩ are small, leaving many noisy coefficients dominated by noise; see Figure 7.10. Donoho and Johnstone systematically developed thresholding estimators based on this observation [17].

Figure 7.10. Denoising using thresholding of wavelet coefficients.

Hard thresholding retains only coefficients whose magnitude exceeds the threshold TTT:

f~=∑∣⟨f, ψm⟩∣>T⟨f, ψm⟩ψm=∑mST(⟨f, ψm⟩)ψm.\tilde f = \sum_{ |\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle|>T } \langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle \psi_m = \sum_{ m } S_T(\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle) \psi_m.f~​=∣⟨f,ψm​⟩∣>T∑​⟨f,ψm​⟩ψm​=m∑​ST​(⟨f,ψm​⟩)ψm​.

where STS_TST​ is defined in (5.4). Retaining the MMM largest noisy coefficients gives the approximation f~=fM\tilde f = f_Mf~​=fM​ of fff. Figure 7.10 illustrates how a suitable TTT removes much of the noise while preserving sharp features.

7.3.2 Soft Thresholding¶

We recall that the hard thresholding operator is defined as

ST(x)=ST0(x)={xif∣x∣>T,0if∣x∣⩽T.(7.8)S_T(x) = S_T^0(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} x \quad \text{if} \quad |x|>T, \\ 0 \quad \text{if} \quad |x|\leqslant T. \end{array} \right. \tag{7.8}ST​(x)=ST0​(x)={xif∣x∣>T,0if∣x∣⩽T.​(7.8)

Hard thresholding makes a discontinuous keep-or-discard decision, which can create artifacts. Soft thresholding is a continuous alternative:

ST1(x)=max⁡(1−T/∣x∣,0)x.(7.9)S_T^1( x ) = \max( 1-T/|x|, 0 ) x. \tag{7.9}ST1​(x)=max(1−T/∣x∣,0)x.(7.9)

Set ST1(0)=0S_T^1(0)=0ST1​(0)=0 by continuity. Figure 7.11 compares the two nonlinear maps.

Figure 7.11. Hard and soft thresholding functions.

For q=0q=0q=0 and q=1q=1q=1, these thresholding rules define two different estimators

f~q=∑mSTq(⟨f, ψm⟩)ψm(7.10)\tilde f^q = \sum_m S_T^q( \langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle ) \psi_m \tag{7.10}f~​q=m∑​STq​(⟨f,ψm​⟩)ψm​(7.10)

Figure 7.12. SNR as a function of T/σT/\sigmaT/σ for hard and soft thresholding.

Preserving coarse-scale coefficients.

Soft thresholding ST1S_T^1ST1​ biases retained coefficients by reducing their magnitudes. Shrinking coarse wavelet coefficients can introduce unwanted low-frequency artifacts. At a coarsest scale 2j02^{j_0}2j0​, it is therefore common to retain the approximation coefficients unchanged. In one dimension, this gives

f~1=∑0⩽n<2−j0⟨f, φj0,n⟩φj0,n+∑j=J+1j0∑0⩽n<2−jST1(⟨f, ψj,n⟩)ψj,n.\tilde f^1 = \sum_{0 \leqslant n < 2^{-j_0}} \langle f,\,\varphi_{j_0,n}\rangle \varphi_{j_0,n} + \sum_{j=J+1}^{j_0}\sum_{0\leqslant n<2^{-j}}S_T^1(\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle)\psi_{j,n}.f~​1=0⩽n<2−j0​∑​⟨f,φj0​,n​⟩φj0​,n​+j=J+1∑j0​​0⩽n<2−j∑​ST1​(⟨f,ψj,n​⟩)ψj,n​.

Empirical choice of the threshold.

Figure 7.12 plots SNR against the threshold TTT for a fixed natural image f0f_0f0​. In this experiment, hard thresholding performs best near T≈3σT \approx 3\sigmaT≈3σ, and soft thresholding near T≈3σ/2T\approx 3\sigma/2T≈3σ/2. The best soft-thresholded estimate has a slightly higher SNR.

Figure 7.13. Comparison of hard (left) and soft (right) thresholding.

These values describe the displayed experiments; the best threshold depends on the image, basis, noise level, and loss function.

7.3.3 Minimax Optimality of Thresholding¶

Estimating sparse coefficients.

To analyze the estimator and guide the choice of TTT, we first assume that the coefficients

a0,m=⟨f0, ψm⟩∈R,a0∈RNa_{0,m}=\langle f_0,\,\psi_m\rangle\in\mathbb{R},\qquad a_0\in\mathbb{R}^Na0,m​=⟨f0​,ψm​⟩∈R,a0​∈RN

are sparse: most entries a0,ma_{0,m}a0,m​ vanish, so the ℓ0\ell^0ℓ0 count

∣ ⁣∣a0∣ ⁣∣0=#{m  ;  a0,m≠0}|\!| a_0 |\!|_0 = \# \left\{ m \;;\; a_{0,m} \neq 0 \right\}∣∣a0​∣∣0​=#{m;a0,m​=0}

is small. As shown in (7.7), noisy coefficients

⟨f, ψm⟩=am=a0,m+zm\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle = a_m = a_{0,m} + z_m⟨f,ψm​⟩=am​=a0,m​+zm​

are perturbed by additive Gaussian white noise of variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. Figure 7.14 shows an example of such a noisy sparse signal.

Figure 7.14. Left: clean sparse coefficients a0a_0a0​; right: noisy coefficients aaa.

Universal threshold value.

When all nonzero clean coefficients are well separated from the noise level, choosing a threshold comparable to the largest pure-noise coefficient suppresses false detections:

T≈τN,τN=max⁡0⩽m<N∣zm∣.T\approx\tau_N,\qquad\tau_N=\max_{0\leqslant m<N}|z_m|.T≈τN​,τN​=0⩽m<Nmax​∣zm​∣.

This motivates a deterministic threshold based on the typical size of τN\tau_NτN​; it is not an exact minimization formula for the realized denoising error. The random maximum τN\tau_NτN​ depends on NNN. For fixed σ\sigmaσ, its mean is asymptotic to σ2log⁡N\sigma\sqrt{2\log N}σ2logN​ as N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞. Its variance tends to zero with NNN, so τN\tau_NτN​ concentrates increasingly near its mean. Figure 7.15 illustrates these trends numerically.

Figure 7.15. Empirical mean (top) and standard deviation (bottom) of the largest absolute Gaussian noise coefficient.

Asymptotic optimality.

Donoho and Johnstone [17] showed that the universal threshold T=σ2log⁡(N)T = \sigma\sqrt{2 \log(N)}T=σ2log(N)​ gives a risk bound for signals that admit accurate nonlinear approximations in {ψm}m\{\psi_m\}_m{ψm​}m​. The risk is within a logarithmic factor of an ideal coefficient-selection risk.

Theorem 7.3

Let N⩾2N\geqslant 2N⩾2 and Y=f0+wY=f_0+wY=f0​+w, with w∼N(0,σ2IN)w\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2I_N)w∼N(0,σ2IN​), in a real orthonormal basis. Hard or soft thresholding (7.10) with

T=σ2ln⁡NT=\sigma\sqrt{2\ln N}T=σ2lnN​

satisfies an oracle inequality of the form

E∣ ⁣∣f0−f~q∣ ⁣∣2⩽C0(1+ln⁡N)[σ2+min⁡0⩽M⩽N(∣ ⁣∣f0−f0,Mnlin∣ ⁣∣2+Mσ2)],\mathbb E|\!| f_0-\tilde f^q |\!|^2 \leqslant C_0(1+\ln N)\left[\sigma^2+\min_{0\leqslant M\leqslant N}\left(|\!| f_0-f_{0,M}^{\mathrm{nlin}} |\!|^2+M\sigma^2\right)\right],E∣∣f0​−f~​q∣∣2⩽C0​(1+lnN)[σ2+0⩽M⩽Nmin​(∣∣f0​−f0,Mnlin​∣∣2+Mσ2)],

where C0C_0C0​ is an absolute constant and f0,Mnlinf_{0,M}^{\mathrm{nlin}}f0,Mnlin​ retains the MMM largest clean coefficients. In particular, if ∣ ⁣∣f0−f0,Mnlin∣ ⁣∣2⩽CM−2β|\!| f_0-f_{0,M}^{\mathrm{nlin}} |\!|^2\leqslant CM^{-2\beta}∣∣f0​−f0,Mnlin​∣∣2⩽CM−2β for 1⩽M⩽N1\leqslant M\leqslant N1⩽M⩽N, with β>0\beta>0β>0, then for 0<σ⩽10<\sigma\leqslant 10<σ⩽1,

E∣ ⁣∣f0−f~q∣ ⁣∣2⩽C′(1+ln⁡N)σ4β/(2β+1),\mathbb E|\!| f_0-\tilde f^q |\!|^2\leqslant C'(1+\ln N)\sigma^{4\beta/(2\beta+1)},E∣∣f0​−f~​q∣∣2⩽C′(1+lnN)σ4β/(2β+1),

where C′C'C′ depends on CCC and β\betaβ.

The oracle inequality is a standard Gaussian thresholding bound; see [17]. The rate follows by balancing CM−2βCM^{-2\beta}CM−2β and Mσ2M\sigma^2Mσ2, with integer rounding and truncation at NNN as in Theorem 7.1. The added σ2\sigma^2σ2 term accounts for residual noise even at the zero signal.

The universal threshold T=σ2ln⁡NT=\sigma\sqrt{2\ln N}T=σ2lnN​ is conservative: it suppresses nearly all pure-noise coefficients. The smaller thresholds illustrated in Figure 7.13 often give better SNR in these experiments.

7.3.4 Translation Invariant Thresholding Estimators¶

Translation invariance.

Let f↦f~=D(f)f\mapsto\tilde f=\mathcal{D}(f)f↦f~​=D(f) be a denoising method, and fτ(x)=f(x−τ)f_\tau(x) = f(x-\tau)fτ​(x)=f(x−τ) be a translated signal or image for τ∈Rd\tau \in \mathbb{R}^dτ∈Rd (d=1d=1d=1 or d=2d=2d=2). The denoiser is translation invariant on the shift lattice Δ\DeltaΔ if

∀ τ∈Δ,D(f)=D(fτ)−τ\forall \,\tau \in \Delta, \quad \mathcal{D}(f) = \mathcal{D}(f_\tau)_{-\tau}∀τ∈Δ,D(f)=D(fτ​)−τ​

where Δ\DeltaΔ is a lattice of Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd. A denser shift lattice imposes equivariance at finer spatial resolution. This corresponds to the fact that D\mathcal{D}D commutes with the translation operator.

Illustration. Unnumbered illustration: cycle spin principle

Translation invariance on a sufficiently fine set Δ\DeltaΔ prevents the denoiser from favoring particular feature locations. Without it, the same feature may be reconstructed differently depending on where it appears, producing visible artifacts.

For denoising by thresholding

D(f)=∑mST(⟨f, ψm⟩)ψm.\mathcal{D}(f) = \sum_m S_T( \langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle ) \psi_m.D(f)=m∑​ST​(⟨f,ψm​⟩)ψm​.

a sufficient condition is invariance of the basis {ψm}m\{\psi_m\}_m{ψm​}m​ under shifts in Δ\DeltaΔ, up to unit-modulus factors:

∀ m′, ∀ τ∈Δ, ∃m, ∃λ∈C,(ψm′)τ=λψm\forall \,m',\ \forall \,\tau\in\Delta,\ \exists m, \: \exists \lambda\in \mathbb{C}, \quad \quad (\psi_{m'})_\tau = \lambda\psi_m∀m′, ∀τ∈Δ, ∃m,∃λ∈C,(ψm′​)τ​=λψm​

where ∣λ∣=1|\lambda|=1∣λ∣=1.

On the periodic domain, the Fourier basis is invariant under every shift Δ=Rd\Delta=\mathbb{R}^dΔ=Rd of [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d. The discrete Fourier basis is invariant under all integer shifts Δ={0,…,N0−1}d\Delta=\{0,\ldots,N_0-1\}^dΔ={0,…,N0​−1}d, where N=N0N=N_0N=N0​ counts samples in one dimension and N=N0×N0N=N_0 \times N_0N=N0​×N0​ counts pixels in two dimensions.

Unfortunately, an orthogonal wavelet basis

{ψm=ψj,n}j,n\{\psi_m = \psi_{j,n} \}_{j,n}{ψm​=ψj,n​}j,n​

is generally not invariant under arbitrary shifts in either the continuous or discrete setting. For instance, in 1-D,

(ψj′,n′)τ∉{ψj,n}forτ=2j′/2.(\psi_{j',n'})_{\tau} \notin \{ \psi_{j,n} \} \quad \text{for} \quad \tau=2^{j\prime}/2.(ψj′,n′​)τ​∈/{ψj,n​}forτ=2j′/2.

Cycle spinning.

For a finite group Δ\DeltaΔ of periodic shifts, average the shifted, denoised, and realigned outputs of D\mathcal{D}D to obtain a translation-invariant estimator:

Dinv(f)=1∣Δ∣∑τ∈ΔD(fτ)−τ.(7.11)\mathcal{D}_{\text{inv}}(f) = \frac{1}{|\Delta|} \sum_{\tau \in \Delta} \mathcal{D}( f_{\tau} )_{-\tau}. \tag{7.11}Dinv​(f)=∣Δ∣1​τ∈Δ∑​D(fτ​)−τ​.(7.11)

One checks that

∀ τ∈Δ,Dinv(f)=Dinv(fτ)−τ\forall \,\tau \in \Delta, \quad \mathcal{D}_{\text{inv}}(f) = \mathcal{D}_{\text{inv}}(f_\tau)_{-\tau}∀τ∈Δ,Dinv​(f)=Dinv​(fτ​)−τ​

To obtain translation invariance at pixel precision for data with NNN samples, one should use a set of ∣Δ∣=N|\Delta|=N∣Δ∣=N translation vectors. For wavelets, this requires O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) operations.

Figure 7.16 applies cycle spinning to hard thresholding in an orthogonal wavelet basis, using the following shifts: Δ={0,1/N0,2/N0,3/N0}2\Delta= \{ 0, 1/N_0, 2/N_0, 3/N_0 \}^2Δ={0,1/N0​,2/N0​,3/N0​}2 on an N0×N0N_0\times N_0N0​×N0​ image, corresponding to shifts by {0,1,2,3}2\{ 0, 1, 2, 3 \}^2{0,1,2,3}2 pixels. This requires 16 forward and inverse wavelet-transform pairs. Averaging this subset of shifts does not in general guarantee exact pixel-shift equivariance. In this example, partial averaging reduces sensitivity to shifts, substantially improves the SNR, and suppresses oscillatory artifacts. These artifacts move as τ\tauτ changes, so averaging reduces them.

In Figure 7.17, translation-invariant hard thresholding slightly outperforms translation-invariant soft thresholding, reversing their ranking in the orthogonal-basis experiment.

Figure 7.16. Soft thresholding in an orthogonal wavelet basis (left) and translation-invariant hard thresholding (right).

Figure 7.17. SNR as a function of T/σT/\sigmaT/σ for translation-invariant thresholding.

Translation invariant wavelet frame.

Cycle spinning also has a frame interpretation: replace the orthogonal basis B={ψm}\mathcal{B}= \{\psi_m\}B={ψm​} by its translated copies,

Binv={(ψm)τ}m,τ∈Δ.(7.12)\mathcal{B}_{\text{inv}} = \{ (\psi_m)_\tau \}_{m, \tau \in \Delta}. \tag{7.12}Binv​={(ψm​)τ​}m,τ∈Δ​.(7.12)

Although Binv\mathcal{B}_{\text{inv}}Binv​ is no longer an orthogonal basis, orthonormality of each translated copy gives the energy and reconstruction identities

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣2=1∣Δ∣∑m,τ∈Δ∣⟨f, (ψm)τ⟩∣2andf=1∣Δ∣∑m,τ∈Δ⟨f, (ψm)τ⟩(ψm)τ.|\!| f |\!|^2 = \frac{1}{|\Delta|} \sum_{m, \tau \in \Delta} |\langle f,\,(\psi_m)_\tau\rangle|^2 \quad \text{and} \quad f = \frac{1}{|\Delta|} \sum_{m, \tau \in \Delta} \langle f,\,(\psi_m)_\tau\rangle (\psi_m)_\tau.∣∣f∣∣2=∣Δ∣1​m,τ∈Δ∑​∣⟨f,(ψm​)τ​⟩∣2andf=∣Δ∣1​m,τ∈Δ∑​⟨f,(ψm​)τ​⟩(ψm​)τ​.

Such redundant families are called tight frames.

One can then define a translation invariant thresholding denoiser

Dinv(f)=1∣Δ∣∑m,τ∈ΔST(⟨f, (ψm)τ⟩)(ψm)τ.(7.13)\mathcal{D}_{\text{inv}}(f) = \frac{1}{|\Delta|} \sum_{m, \tau \in \Delta} S_T(\langle f,\,(\psi_m)_\tau\rangle) (\psi_m)_\tau. \tag{7.13}Dinv​(f)=∣Δ∣1​m,τ∈Δ∑​ST​(⟨f,(ψm​)τ​⟩)(ψm​)τ​.(7.13)

This estimator equals the cycle spinning estimator defined in (7.11).

Counted with multiplicity, the translated frame has ∣Δ∣∣B∣|\Delta| |\mathcal{B}|∣Δ∣∣B∣ elements. For a basis of signals with NNN samples and a lattice of ∣Δ∣=N|\Delta|=N∣Δ∣=N shifts, this gives up to N2N^2N2 vectors in Binv\mathcal{B}_{\text{inv}}Binv​. In a hierarchical construction such as a wavelet basis, however, different shifts can produce the same atom:

(ψm)τ=(ψm′)τ′form≠m′andτ≠τ′,(\psi_m)_\tau = (\psi_{m'})_{\tau'} \quad \text{for} \quad m \neq m' \quad \text{and} \quad \tau\neq \tau',(ψm​)τ​=(ψm′​)τ′​form=m′andτ=τ′,

The number of distinct vectors in Binv\mathcal{B}_{\text{inv}}Binv​ can therefore be much smaller than N2N^2N2. For instance, for an orthogonal wavelet basis, one has

(ψj,n)k2j=ψj,n+k,(\psi_{j,n})_{k 2^j} = \psi_{j,n+k},(ψj,n​)k2j​=ψj,n+k​,

so many translated atoms coincide. For a signal of length NNN, an undecimated transform has log⁡2N\log_2Nlog2​N detail arrays of length NNN, plus a coarse array. For an N0×N0N_0\times N_0N0​×N0​ image (N=N02N=N_0^2N=N02​), it has 3log⁡2N03\log_2N_03log2​N0​ detail arrays of NNN entries, plus a coarse array. Appropriate multiplicity weights must be retained when replacing the full translated family by distinct atoms.

The fast undecimated wavelet transform, often called the “à trous” transform, computes these coefficients in O(Nlog⁡N)O(N\log N)O(NlogN) operations. Each detail array is indexed directly by every pixel location:

djω[n]=⟨f, (ψj,0ω)n⟩,n∈{0,…,N0−1}2,ω∈{V,H,D},d_j^\omega[n]=\langle f,\,(\psi_{j,0}^\omega)_n\rangle,\qquad n\in\{0,\ldots,N_0-1\}^2,\quad\omega\in\{V,H,D\},djω​[n]=⟨f,(ψj,0ω​)n​⟩,n∈{0,…,N0​−1}2,ω∈{V,H,D},

where the wavelets and shifts are discrete and appropriately normalized. Each array is a band-pass filtered image, as illustrated in Figure 7.18.

7.3.5 Other Shrinkage Rules¶

Other shrinkage rules offer different compromises between retaining large coefficients and suppressing noise. We describe two examples whose performance depends on the coefficient distribution of fff in the chosen basis.

Semi-soft thresholding.

Semi-soft thresholding interpolates between hard and soft thresholding through a parameter μ>1\mu>1μ>1:

STθ(x)=g11−θ(x)wheregμ(x)={0if∣x∣<Txif∣x∣>μTsign(x)μ(∣x∣−T)μ−1 otherwise.S_T^\theta(x) = g_{\frac{1}{1-\theta}}(x) \quad \text{where} \quad g_\mu(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \quad \text{if} \quad |x|<T\\ x \quad \text{if} \quad |x|>\mu T\\ \mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(x)\frac{\mu(|x|-T)}{\mu-1} \text{ otherwise.} \end{array} \right.STθ​(x)=g1−θ1​​(x)wheregμ​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​0if∣x∣<Txif∣x∣>μTsign(x)μ−1μ(∣x∣−T)​ otherwise.​

For 0<θ<10<\theta<10<θ<1, set μ=1/(1−θ)\mu=1/(1-\theta)μ=1/(1−θ). The limits θ↓0\theta\downarrow0θ↓0 and θ↑1\theta\uparrow1θ↑1 give hard and soft thresholding, respectively, away from the threshold boundary. Figure 7.20 shows an example of this nonlinearity.

Figure 7.20. Left: semi-soft thresholder, right: Stein thresholder.

Figure 7.21 shows an SNR improvement for a suitable choice of μ\muμ, although the visual difference from hard and soft thresholding is small.

Figure 7.21. Left: SNR as a function of μ\muμ and T/σT/\sigmaT/σ. Right: SNR versus μ\muμ, with T/σT/\sigmaT/σ optimized separately for each μ\muμ.

Stein thresholding.

Stein thresholding is defined using a quadratic attenuation of large coefficients

STStein(x)=max⁡(1−T2∣x∣2,0)x.S_T^{\text{Stein}}(x) = \max\left( 1-\frac{T^2}{|x|^2},0 \right)x.STStein​(x)=max(1−∣x∣2T2​,0)x.

The value at x=0x=0x=0 is defined to be zero. This should be compared with the linear attenuation of soft thresholding

ST1(x)=max⁡(1−T∣x∣,0)x.S_T^1(x) = \max\left( 1-\frac{T}{|x|},0 \right)x.ST1​(x)=max(1−∣x∣T​,0)x.

For large coefficients, Stein thresholding has the following shrinkage behavior:

∣STStein(x)−x∣→0 whereas ∣ST1(x)−x∣→T,|S_T^{\text{Stein}}(x)-x| \rightarrow 0 \quad\text{ whereas }\quad |S_T^1(x)-x| \rightarrow T,∣STStein​(x)−x∣→0 whereas ∣ST1​(x)−x∣→T,

as x→±∞x \rightarrow \pm \inftyx→±∞. Its deterministic shrinkage tends to zero, whereas soft thresholding retains a fixed shrinkage. This limiting property does not imply unbiased estimation at finite amplitudes.

Figure 7.22. SNR as a function of T/σT/\sigmaT/σ for Stein thresholding.

Stein and hard thresholding give similar results in the translation-invariant natural-image experiments shown here.

7.3.6 Block Thresholding¶

The nonlinear thresholding methods above are diagonal estimators, since they attenuate each coefficient separately

f~=∑mATq(⟨f, ψm⟩)⟨f, ψm⟩ψm\tilde f = \sum_m A_T^q(\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle) \langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle \psi_mf~​=m∑​ATq​(⟨f,ψm​⟩)⟨f,ψm​⟩ψm​

where

ATq(x)={max⁡(1−T2/∣x∣2,0)forq=Steinmax⁡(1−T/∣x∣,0)forq=1 (soft)1∣x∣>Tforq=0 (hard)A_T^q(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \max(1-T^2/|x|^2,0) \quad \text{for} \quad q=\text{Stein}\\ \max(1-T/|x|,0) \quad \text{for} \quad q=1\text{ (soft)}\\ 1_{|x|>T} \quad \text{for} \quad q=0\text{ (hard)} \end{array} \right.ATq​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​max(1−T2/∣x∣2,0)forq=Steinmax(1−T/∣x∣,0)forq=1 (soft)1∣x∣>T​forq=0 (hard)​

Define every attenuation factor to be zero at x=0x=0x=0 when T>0T>0T>0. Block thresholding shares an attenuation factor across a group of coefficients, exploiting their statistical dependence. This is useful for natural images, where edges create clusters of large wavelet coefficients. Grouping also helps suppress isolated noise coefficients in otherwise smooth regions.

Partition the coefficients into disjoint blocks; for example, in a 2-D wavelet transform,

{(j,n,ω)}j,n,ω=⋃kBk,\{ (j,n,\omega) \}_{j,n,\omega} = \bigcup_k B_k,{(j,n,ω)}j,n,ω​=k⋃​Bk​,

where each BkB_kBk​ contains s×ss\times ss×s neighboring coefficients at a fixed scale and orientation. The block size sss is a parameter of the method. Figure 7.23 shows an example of such a block.

The mean squared coefficient magnitude in a block is

Ek=1∣Bk∣∑m∈Bk∣⟨f, ψm⟩∣2.E_k=\frac{1}{|B_k|} \sum_{ m \in B_k } |\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle|^2.Ek​=∣Bk​∣1​m∈Bk​∑​∣⟨f,ψm​⟩∣2.

The block estimator

f~=∑mSTblock,q(⟨f, ψm⟩)ψm\tilde f = \sum_m S_T^{\text{block},q}(\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle) \psi_mf~​=m∑​STblock,q​(⟨f,ψm​⟩)ψm​

applies the same attenuation to every coefficient in a block,

∀ m∈Bk,STblock,q(⟨f, ψm⟩)=ATq(Ek)⟨f, ψm⟩,\forall \,m \in B_k, \quad S_T^{\text{block},q} (\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle) = A_T^q(\sqrt{E_k}) \langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle,∀m∈Bk​,STblock,q​(⟨f,ψm​⟩)=ATq​(Ek​​)⟨f,ψm​⟩,

for q∈{0,1,stein}q \in \{0,1,\text{stein}\}q∈{0,1,stein}. Figure 7.23 shows the attenuated blocks and the reconstructed image.

Figure 7.23. Left: wavelet coefficients, center: block thresholded coefficients, right: denoised image.

Figure 7.24, left, compares the rules for q∈{0,1,stein}q \in \{0,1,\text{stein}\}q∈{0,1,stein}. Stein block thresholding gives the highest SNR in this comparison. Figure 7.24, right, compares block sizes for Stein thresholding. The choice s=4s=4s=4 performs well in the displayed experiment.

Figure 7.24. SNR as a function of T/σT/\sigmaT/σ (left) and comparison of different block sizes (right).

Figure 7.25 compares the reconstructions. Stein block thresholding in an orthogonal wavelet basis approaches the quality of translation-invariant hard thresholding here, at lower computational cost. The block thresholding strategy can also be applied to wavelet coefficients in a translation invariant tight frame, which gives the best result among the methods compared in this experiment.

The same block attenuation can be implemented directly after the wavelet transform.

Figure 7.25. Left: translation invariant wavelet hard thresholding, center: block orthogonal Stein thresholding, right: block translation invariant Stein thresholding.

More advanced denoisers use richer statistical models to improve on the methods presented here; see, for instance, [27].

7.4 Signal-Dependent Noise¶

In many imaging systems, the variance of the noise affecting f0,nf_{0,n}f0,n​ depends on the intensity f0,nf_{0,n}f0,n​ itself. We now study Poisson counts and multiplicative noise. Both can be expressed as additive residuals, but their residual distributions depend on the signal.

7.4.1 Poisson Noise¶

Many imaging devices measure intensity by counting photons. Examples include digital cameras, confocal microscopy, PET and SPECT tomography.

Poisson model.

For an unknown mean intensity f0,n⩾0f_{0,n}\geqslant 0f0,n​⩾0, a Poisson model describes the observed photon count:

fn∼P(λ)whereλ=f0,n∈[0,∞),f_n \sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda) \quad \text{where} \quad \lambda=f_{0,n}\in[0,\infty),fn​∼P(λ)whereλ=f0,n​∈[0,∞),

The Poisson distribution P(λ)\mathcal{P}(\lambda)P(λ) has probability mass function

P(fn=k)=λke−λk!\mathbb{P}(f_n=k)=\frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}P(fn​=k)=k!λke−λ​

and its parameter varies across pixels with the underlying intensity. Figure 7.26 shows several Poisson distributions.

Figure 7.26. Poisson distributions for various λ\lambdaλ.

One has

E(fn)=λ=f0,nandVar(fn)=λ=f0,n\mathbb E(f_n)=\lambda=f_{0,n} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{Var}(f_n)=\lambda=f_{0,n}E(fn​)=λ=f0,n​andVar(fn​)=λ=f0,n​

Thus denoising again estimates a mean from one observation, but the variance now varies with intensity. The absolute noise level increases as more photons reach the sensor. For positive intensity, the relative standard deviation f0,n−1/2f_{0,n}^{-1/2}f0,n−1/2​ instead decreases.

Figure 7.27 shows Poisson-corrupted versions of a clean image f0f_0f0​ at different maximum mean intensities λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​.

Figure 7.27. Poisson-corrupted flower images at increasing photon-count scales λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​.

Variance stabilization.

Applying a thresholding estimator

D(f)=∑mSTq(⟨f, ψm⟩)ψm\mathcal{D}(f) = \sum_m S_T^q(\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle) \psi_mD(f)=m∑​STq​(⟨f,ψm​⟩)ψm​

directly to fff can perform poorly because a single threshold TTT cannot adapt to spatially varying noise. A variance-stabilizing transform φ:[0,+∞)→R\varphi: [0,+\infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}φ:[0,+∞)→R, applied pixelwise, maps the counts to φ(f)\varphi(f)φ(f). An additive Gaussian white-noise model can then be a useful approximation:

φ(f)≈φ(f0)+w(7.14)\varphi(f) \approx \varphi(f_0) + w \tag{7.14}φ(f)≈φ(f0​)+w(7.14)

where wn∼N(0,σ2)w_n\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)wn​∼N(0,σ2) are independent centered Gaussians with constant variance σ2\sigma^2σ2.

The model (7.14) is approximate, and its accuracy depends on the intensity range of f0,nf_{0,n}f0,n​. Two common variance-stabilizing transforms for Poisson noise are the Anscombe transform

φ(x)=2x+3/8\varphi(x) = 2\sqrt{x+3/8}φ(x)=2x+3/8​

and the Freeman–Tukey transform

φ(x)=x+1+x.\varphi(x) = \sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{x}.φ(x)=x+1​+x​.

Figure 7.28 compares the variance of φ(f)\varphi(f)φ(f) after these transformations.

Figure 7.28. Exact Poisson variances of the Anscombe, Freeman–Tukey, and 2x2\sqrt{x}2x​ transforms as functions of the mean intensity.

A variance-stabilized denoiser is defined as

Dstab,q(f)=φ−1(∑mSTq(⟨φ(f), ψm⟩)ψm)\mathcal{D}^{\text{stab},q}(f) = \varphi^{-1}( \sum_m S_T^q(\langle \varphi(f),\,\psi_m\rangle) \psi_m )Dstab,q(f)=φ−1(m∑​STq​(⟨φ(f),ψm​⟩)ψm​)

where φ−1\varphi^{-1}φ−1 is applied after projecting the denoised values onto its domain. The direct inverse generally introduces bias, especially at low counts; bias-corrected inverse transforms can improve the result.

At the moderate count levels in Figure 7.29, variance stabilization improves the denoising result.

Figure 7.29. Left: noisy image, center: denoising without variance stabilization, right: denoising after variance stabilization.

7.4.2 Multiplicative Noise¶

Multiplicative image formation.

A multiplicative noise model assumes that

fn=f0,nwnf_n = f_{0,n} w_nfn​=f0,n​wn​

where www is a random multiplier, observed through one realization, with E(wn)=1\mathbb E(w_n)=1E(wn​)=1. Once again, the noise level depends on the pixel value

E(fn)=f0,nandVar(fn)=f0,n2σ2whereσ2=Var⁡(wn).\mathbb E(f_n) = f_{0,n} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{Var}(f_n) = f_{0,n}^2 \sigma^2 \quad \text{where} \quad \sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(w_n).E(fn​)=f0,n​andVar(fn​)=f0,n2​σ2whereσ2=Var(wn​).

In SAR imaging, a common model forms fff by averaging KKK independent observations, called looks:

∀ 1⩽s⩽K,fn(s)=f0,nwn(s)+rn(s)\forall \,1\leqslant s\leqslant K, \quad f^{(s)}_n = f_{0,n} w^{(s)}_n + r^{(s)}_n∀1⩽s⩽K,fn(s)​=f0,n​wn(s)​+rn(s)​

where r(s)r^{(s)}r(s) is additive Gaussian white noise and the multiplier wn(s)w^{(s)}_nwn(s)​ has an exponential distribution:

pwn(s)(x)=e−x1x>0.p_{w^{(s)}_n}(x)=e^{-x}\mathbf1_{x>0}.pwn(s)​​(x)=e−x1x>0​.

Averaging KKK independent looks divides the additive-noise variance by KKK. When the remaining additive component is negligible, the average is approximately

fn=1K∑s=1Kfn(s)≈f0,nwnf_n = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{s=1}^K f^{(s)}_n \approx f_{0,n} w_nfn​=K1​s=1∑K​fn(s)​≈f0,n​wn​

where the multiplicative factor is distributed according to a Gamma distribution

wn∼Gamma⁡(shape=K,rate=K),pwn(x)=KKΓ(K)xK−1e−Kx1x>0.w_n\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\text{shape}=K,\text{rate}=K),\qquad p_{w_n}(x)=\frac{K^K}{\Gamma(K)}x^{K-1}e^{-Kx}\mathbf1_{x>0}.wn​∼Gamma(shape=K,rate=K),pwn​​(x)=Γ(K)KK​xK−1e−Kx1x>0​.

Its mean is one and its variance is 1/K1/K1/K, so increasing KKK reduces the relative noise level.

Figure 7.30. Multiplicative Gamma noise for increasing numbers KKK of averaged looks, with standard deviation σ=K−1/2\sigma=K^{-1/2}σ=K−1/2.

Figure 7.30 illustrates how the noise changes with the number K=1/σ2K=1/\sigma^2K=1/σ2 of averaged looks.

A simple variance stabilization transform is

φ(x)=log⁡(x)−c\varphi(x)=\log(x) - cφ(x)=log(x)−c

where

c=E(log⁡(w))=ψ(K)−log⁡(K)whereψ(x)=Γ′(x)/Γ(x)c = \text{E}(\log(w)) = \psi(K) - \log(K) \quad \text{where} \quad \psi(x) = \Gamma'(x)/\Gamma(x)c=E(log(w))=ψ(K)−log(K)whereψ(x)=Γ′(x)/Γ(x)

Here Γ\GammaΓ is the Gamma function and ψ\psiψ is its logarithmic derivative, the digamma function. The transformed observation satisfies

φ(f)n=log⁡f0,n+zn,\varphi(f)_n=\log f_{0,n}+z_n,φ(f)n​=logf0,n​+zn​,

for strictly positive intensities, where zn=log⁡(wn)−cz_n=\log(w_n)-czn​=log(wn​)−c is centered additive noise with variance ψ(1)(K)\psi^{(1)}(K)ψ(1)(K); ψ(1)\psi^{(1)}ψ(1) is the derivative of the digamma function. Thus the transformed target is log⁡f0\log f_0logf0​, not φ(f0)\varphi(f_0)φ(f0​). Exponentiating an estimate of log⁡f0\log f_0logf0​ introduces a further statistical bias and may require correction.
